Hardtail MTBs Are Still In: This Designer Shows Off What His Idea of Cycling Perfection Looks Like
7 photos
Photo: Sergey Fedotov
The decades have been subject to countless designs based around the timeless bicycle. So much so that it can be considered one of the most looked-at of vehicles, next to cars and motorcycles, that is. Well, one thing that all real bicycles have in common is that they started off as a dream or a concept, and today, we dive deeper into one such concept.
Bicycles have been around for over 100 years, and in that time, have been subject to take after take on what it means to be the most efficient and capable machine out there, and it all comes down to the backbone , or frame.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Frames come in countless shapes, designs, and abilities, not to mention materials or building blocks to give rise to those traits. Some are completed from steel, some from aluminum, and the more exotic ones, from carbon fiber and titanium.
But, most bicycles have always followed the traditional double-diamond frame, with a rhombus shape split into two triangles by a seat post. Road bikes follow this design, and so do gravel bikes and hardtail MTBs. The exception are full-suspension MTBs, which break the rear wheel away from the frame to grant it dampening abilities.
As a result of all these and more, it’s important to note that all bikes are designed for a particular discipline. It’s why you don’t see road bikes flying down mountain sides and grandma cruisers in the same setting. But, it’s also why MTBs don’t excel on roads either.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Some frames and bicycle designs have sought to bridge the gap between roads and mountainsides, with one of the most recent being the gravel bike. Gravel bikes are somewhere between a hardtail MTB and a road bike, often spotted with drop bars, for an aerodynamic rider position, and a dropped seat stay to soften up the rear.
While the traditional gravel bike doesn’t have a front suspension, these days, some brands have added suspension forks to their gravel bikes. It’s not much – usually about 30 mm or so – but it is enough to help us break away from the tarmac and gravel road and venture a bit deeper into the woods and hit up light trails.
Up until gravel bikes, it was the hardtail that was often the most called-upon of frame styles for the all-around rider, and some brands still use this frame style as the starting point for their very modern bikes. Even Trek, Cannondale, Scott, Giant, and countless others still produce hardtails.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Often, these bad boys are equipped with a front suspension fork with a minimum of 80 mm and with a lockout function, can be set to transfer all of your pedaling energy into the rear wheel.
That brings us to the concept before us today, one crafted by Sergey Fedotov and built to represent the Stern brand. Stern is a Russian brand that hit the scene back in 2005, so they’ve been around for well over 20 years, and the FVA, as Fedotov calls it, is “ conceived as a special-edition model ,” so we could very well see Stern taking a crack at this one some day.
As we can see, Fedotov called upon the hardtail design to bring the FVA to life, and another trait that I could make out is that it’s built out of nothing but good old carbon fiber. There are no welds anywhere on the bike and long flowing tubes are also a trait of carbon fiber frames. A traditional double-diamond design is present here.
What I can also make out is that Fedotov knows what it takes to craft a solid MTB, integrating a tapered head tube into the mix and designing the frame with a “racing geometry.” It’s also built around 29-inch wheels.
Photo: Sergey Fedotov Fedotov also calls upon some of the industry’s most revered and proven materials . For example, the fork is a RockShox SID SL Ultimate with 100 mm, and the drivetrain is meant to carry the Shimano name. Shimano is also responsible for a pair of hydraulic disc brakes with 180 and 160 mm rotors. Ritchey can also be spotted all over, a name present on the handlebar, stem, and seatpost.
What I found rather interesting is that Fedotov did NOT equip this concept with the most expensive gear out there, leaving some room for growth, which could be a clear indicator that he is designing this one for the masses and not tossing on wallet-wrenching gear. Without the pedals, the entire setup aims for a total weight of 11 kg (24 lbs).
The question is: How much would someone like you and me pay for a concept of this nature? Well, taking into consideration that a carbon fiber frame is called upon, a fork that costs around $1,000, and a drivetrain of around the same price, I’d say that this one would be going for around $5,000, a price that some folks would consider dropping on a carbon fiber hardtail MTB.
How much would you pay for such a ride ?
